title: Apple's Siri AI Can Be Swapped Out for Claude, ChatGPT, Code Shows
content:
Code sleuth "pdfu" has uncovered iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate private frameworks that show Apple has designed its new Siri architecture to work with third-party AI models at what appears to be a surprisingly deep level.
One mechanism called Model Delegation allows Claude to appear as a Siri extension in the same way as the existing built-in ChatGPT extension. In pdf's video, shared on X, the macOS user brings up the "Search or Ask" bar and chooses Claude as the AI model via an "Ask..." contextual menu. 
After enabling the Claude extension, the user asks Siri to "Ask Claude" to set a reminder in Apple's Reminders app. Claude then interprets the natural language reminder request and Siri subsequently creates the reminder. The implication is that if the request requires access to an Apple system feature, Claude hands the task back to Siri.
In another example, Claude can be seen in a Siri app conversation window receiving a request to create a CSV file – something Siri itself cannot handle – and successfully returning the result.
What's more intriguing is the second protocol demonstrated in the video that appears to go considerably further, and could really open up the AI landscape for Apple software requests.
An inference provider in "Model Manager Services" apparently allows Apple's own server-side Siri model to be completely replaced by another model, such as GPT-5.6. In this scenario, ChatGPT receives Apple's Siri planner prompt and tool definitions, which enables it to request system actions, receive the resulting personal data, and formulate an answer that Siri presents using its own interface and voice.
And here's an app extension replacing Siri AI's server model with GPT-5.6 Terra. It uses the Inference Providing protocol in Model Manager Services. GPT-5.6 receives Apple's native Siri planner prompt and tool definitions. It can make tool calls that perform system actions, and... pic.twitter.com/cz88kyq3io — pdfu (@itspdfu) September 13, 2026
In the demonstration video, the user asks the ChatGPT model (within the Siri app) to find emails about a specific topic, summarize their contents and action points, then send an message to a person in the user's contacts via the Messages app. The response is then shown as logged in OpenAI's platform web interface.
The European Union's Digital Markets Act may have helped shape Apple's approach here, as it requires Apple to give third parties effective access to iOS hardware and software features available to Apple's own services, and the European Commission has specifically said this principle extends to Siri.
The "Ask..." implementation is currently limited to the ChatGPT extension in the macOS 27 Golden Gate Release Candidate (which is effectively the final version of the software set to be released later today), so Claude is not yet available. Meanwhile, Apple has not yet opened up the model delegation entitlement to third parties and it isn't front-facing to users, but it at least shows how extensively Apple has engineered Siri for future model interoperability.

report.summary: Leaked iOS 27 code shows Siri can hand tasks to Claude and even let GPT-5.6 replace Apple's own server-side model, hinting at deep third-party AI integration.
report.background: Apple has been rebuilding Siri around large language models after years of criticism that it lagged behind ChatGPT and Gemini, and it already shipped a ChatGPT extension inside Apple Intelligence. Meanwhile, the EU's Digital Markets Act requires Apple to give third parties effective access to iOS features available to its own services — a principle the European Commission has said explicitly extends to Siri. Against that regulatory backdrop, Apple appears to have architected Siri as a pluggable shell rather than a single closed model, preparing for a future where users pick their assistant's brain while Apple retains control of the interface, system permissions, and personal data plumbing.
key_points: Model Delegation lets a third-party model behave like a Siri extension. In a demo, a user selects Claude from the 'Search or Ask' bar and asks Siri to 'Ask Claude' to set a reminder. Claude parses the natural-language request, but Siri performs the actual system action, with tasks handed back whenever Apple features are needed.

A deeper protocol, Inference Providing in Model Manager Services, allows Apple's server-side Siri model to be swapped out entirely. ChatGPT receives Apple's own Siri planner prompt and tool definitions, so it can request system actions, read the resulting personal data, and produce an answer that Siri presents in its own interface and voice.

The demonstration shows capabilities Siri alone cannot handle: Claude generates a CSV file inside a Siri conversation, while the swapped-in ChatGPT model finds and summarizes emails, extracts action points, and sends a message to a contact via Messages — with the exchange logged in OpenAI's platform web interface.

The EU's Digital Markets Act likely shaped this design. It obliges Apple to grant third parties effective access to iOS hardware and software features available to Apple's own services, and the European Commission has specifically said that requirement extends to Siri.

Nothing is live yet. The 'Ask...' menu is limited to the ChatGPT extension in the macOS 27 Golden Gate release candidate, Claude is not yet available, and Apple has not opened the model delegation entitlement to third parties or exposed any of it to users.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes Siri from a competitor into a distribution channel: model makers could bid for the assistant layer on a billion devices while Apple keeps the interface, permissions, and data mediation. For developers, the entitlement structure matters more than the demos — if Apple opens Model Delegation and Inference Providing beyond ChatGPT, building a Siri-compatible model becomes a real market, but only on Apple's terms and only if regulators keep pushing. For regular users, the practical upside is a Siri that stops refusing hard tasks and hands them to a capable model, though it also raises sharp questions about which company sees your emails, reminders, and messages, and whether that visibility is disclosed clearly.
report.tools: Worth watching: Apple's App Intents and Foundation Models frameworks, which define how extensions and tool calls plug into Siri, plus the Model Manager Services entitlement if it opens up. For experimenting locally with swappable models, try Ollama, llama.cpp or LM Studio for on-device inference, Open WebUI as a pluggable chat front end, and tool-calling orchestration layers like LangChain or LlamaIndex. Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's API docs are the reference points for the delegation behavior shown.
